tagline: An old stage-road alignment links the county seat and its schools.
intro: New Kent Highway narrows from four divided lanes near I-64 to an undivided two-lane road as it curves east. It crosses a county of wooded and agricultural rolling hills, with the Pamunkey River defining the northeastern border and the Chickahominy the southwestern one.

The western 11 miles of SR 249 roughly follow the Richmond-Williamsburg Stage Road, heavily used by Confederate and Union troops during the Peninsula Campaign in 1862. As I-64 was being built east of Richmond, nearby SR 33 carried heavy weekend traffic toward waterfront destinations in eastern Virginia and had a high accident rate. The SR 249 number came in the early 1970s, assigned to a former section of SR 33. SR 33 was rerouted onto I-64, leaving its old alignment as northern New Kent County's main local highway.

Heading east, the highway passes Quinton and reaches the SR 106 roundabout at Talleysville. Beyond Carps Corner comes New Kent, with its courthouse and schools. SR 249 ends at Angelview Church, where SR 30 and SR 33 meet; SR 30 continues southeast toward Williamsburg. At that final junction, SR 33 follows Eltham Road, with SR 30 joining it toward West Point; the southeast branch continues the New Kent Highway name.

moments.title: Crump's Mill
moments.text: Crump's Mill stands behind the dam of an L-shaped millpond near Talleysville, on private property. Damming South Branch in the early nineteenth century created the pond. The present mill dates to the 1870s. Its predecessor, built before 1818, burned in 1872; the replacement operated until 1955. A rectangular, two-story frame building with a gable roof, it retains much of its milling machinery.

moments.title: St. Peter's Church
moments.text: Curved gable ends and a brick tower distinguish St. Peter's Church near Talleysville. Construction began in 1701 and finished in 1703, supervised by vestryman Colonel Joseph Foster. Its rector, Rev. David Mossom, married Martha Custis and George Washington in 1759, but the ceremony's location remains disputed between the church and White House Plantation. Union soldiers later stabled horses in the pews and carved their names into the exterior brickwork. Much of the building has since been restored or replaced. The tower's open arches, pyramidal roof and four original stuccoed brick urns are part of its exterior.
moments.notice: St. Peter's Church has curved gable ends and a brick tower topped with four stuccoed urns.

moments.title: Former New Kent High School
moments.text: Before desegregation, New Kent High School served white students while George W. Watkins served African American students. Dr. Calvin C. Green led the push for desegregation in Green v. County School Board. In 1968, the Supreme Court ruled that the county's freedom-of-choice plan failed to provide prompt, meaningful desegregation. After the ruling, the school board adopted integration by grade level, consolidating elementary grades at Watkins and secondary grades at New Kent. The two schools became a National Historic Landmark in 2001. The former New Kent campus now serves Rappahannock Community College; the school district built a new high school south of it.
